content: 1. Biological Impurity: A biological impurity refers to any biological entity or its components, excluding chemical contaminants, that arise during the production of an active ingredient derived from a biological source. This definition does not include impurities originating from formulants or other additives. For further clarification, refer to the terms Contaminant and Relevant Impurity. 2. Chemical Impurity: A chemical impurity is a by-product formed during the manufacturing of an active ingredient or derived from the active ingredient during formulation or storage. This definition excludes impurities solely originating from formulants or other additives, either before or during storage. See also Contaminant and Relevant Impurity. 3. INCI Number: The International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients (INCI) number is a standardized identifier for cosmetic ingredients. 4. Independent Laboratory Validation: This refers to the validation of an analytical method by a laboratory that operates independently from the originator of the method. This process ensures the reliability and reproducibility of the method without any collusion between the parties involved. 5. Interested Parties: These include organizations or individuals, such as commercial companies, pesticide registration authorities, non-governmental organizations, and scientists, who are concerned with pesticide specifications. 6. ISO: The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) publishes common names for pesticides, often developed by the British Standards Institution (BSI). The English form of the name is denoted as E-ISO, while the French form is denoted as F-ISO, with gender (masculine or feminine) specified as appropriate. 7. IUPAC: The International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) is an organization that standardizes chemical nomenclature and terminology. 8. Lot: A lot refers to part or all of a consignment that may consist of one or more manufacturing batches. 9. Lump: A lump is a macroscopic piece of solid matter that lacks a regular shape. 10. Manual: The manual refers to the current edition or revision of the FAO/WHO Manual on the development and use of specifications for pesticides. 11. Manufacturer: A manufacturer is any entity, whether public or private, engaged in the production of a pesticide active ingredient. This includes direct production or production through agents or contracted entities. 12. Manufacturing Specification: This specifies the minimum purity of the active ingredient in a technical-grade product, along with the identity and maximum concentrations of all impurities, including unknowns, based on representative production batches. Impurities with limits of 1 g/kg or higher are generally included, with lower limits applied for exceptionally hazardous impurities. 13. Minimum Data Requirements: These are the essential data needed to evaluate proposals for FAO/WHO specifications, ensuring all aspects of the specification are adequately assessed. 14. Non-Flammable: A substance is considered non-flammable if it is not readily ignitable and has a flash point above 55°C, as determined by a closed-cup method. 15. Open Meeting: An open meeting is jointly organized by JMPS and CIPAC, allowing participation from anyone interested, in addition to experts invited by FAO/WHO. 16. Oversize Particles: These are particles of solid material that exceed a specified size. 17. Peer Validation: Also known as independent laboratory validation, this involves the validation of an analytical method by a laboratory operating independently from the originator. The process follows established peer verification procedures, such as those of AOAC International. 18. Pesticide: A pesticide is any chemical or biological substance, or a mixture thereof, intended to repel, destroy, or control pests, or regulate plant growth. This includes substances used to control vectors of human or animal diseases, nuisance pests, or unwanted plant or animal species that interfere with food production, storage, or marketing. It also encompasses substances used as insect or plant growth regulators, defoliants, desiccants, or agents for fruit thinning or setting. 19. Phytotoxic: Phytotoxicity refers to the ability of a compound to cause temporary or long-lasting damage to plants. This damage may be general or specific to certain plant species or cultivars. Phytotoxic impurities in herbicides can extend the range of plant damage beyond what is expected. 20. Proposer: A proposer is any manufacturer, group of manufacturers, or interested party that submits a draft specification and data package to FAO/WHO for evaluation, either for a new specification or an extension of an existing one. 21. Reference Specification: This is the initial specification used to determine the equivalence of a technical-grade active ingredient or formulation from a subsequent manufacturer. It is subject to review and may be revised based on new information or additional formulations. 22. Reference Profile: The reference profile includes the purity, impurity, toxicological, and ecotoxicological data upon which the original specification for a technical-grade active ingredient is based. It is used to determine equivalence and is not amended by data from additional equivalent active ingredients. 23. Release Date: The release date is the date from which the supplier guarantees a shelf life of at least two years under actual storage conditions in the intended marketing area. 24. Relevant Impurity: A relevant impurity is a by-product of pesticide manufacture or storage that is toxicologically significant to health or the environment, phytotoxic to treated plants, causes taint in food crops, affects pesticide stability, or has other adverse effects. Water and insoluble materials may also be relevant impurities if they impact stability or formulation performance. 25. Risk: Risk is the probability of an adverse effect occurring in an organism, system, or population under specified conditions due to exposure to an agent. 26. Sedimentation: Sedimentation refers to the settling of particles in a continuous medium, typically a liquid. 27. Sieving: Sieving is the process of separating particles based on size using sieves. 28. Size Distribution: This describes the mass or numerical frequency distribution of particles in a solid particulate material. 29. Size Range: The size range defines the lower and upper size limits of a particulate material. 30. Specification: A specification outlines the parameters and criteria defining the physical and chemical properties of technical and formulated pesticides, linked to their hazard and risk profiles. 31. Subsequent Manufacturer: This refers to any pesticide manufacturer other than the proposer of the original specification. 32. Surfactant: A surfactant is a formulant that reduces interfacial tension between two surfaces, enhancing emulsifying, spreading, dispersibility, and/or wetting properties of liquids or solids. 33. Tolerance: Tolerance refers to the permitted variation limits for active ingredient content from a specified value, also known as certified limits in some countries. 34. Toxicity: Toxicity is the inherent property of a substance to cause adverse biological effects. 35. Toxicological Profile: This is a summary of data on toxicological endpoints that may impact human health due to exposure to a specific pesticide through various routes. 36. Undersize Particles: These are particles of solid material smaller than a specified size. 37. Validation: Validation is the process of establishing the reliability and relevance of a particular method, process, or assessment for a defined purpose. 38. WHO: The World Health Organization (WHO) is a specialized agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health. 39. WHOPES: The WHO Pesticide Evaluation Scheme evaluates pesticides for public health use. 40. ISO Coding of Active Ingredients: ISO common names are used in specifications and analytical methods, where possible. Each specification or CIPAC method is assigned a number based on the CIPAC code for the chemical and its derivatives, facilitating identification and retrieval.
